I shipped my first e-commerce store with zero budget for premium plugins.

Most people think starting a brand requires a massive investment in software or a ready-made suite of tools. When we started Prettiva and Co, we had literally nothing but an idea and a laptop.

I ended up writing custom scripts to handle simple inventory logic because the available paid plugins were either too expensive or overkill for what we needed.

That limitation turned into a massive advantage. I learned exactly how the data flow works behind the checkout screen instead of just clicking install on a dashboard.

Sometimes having access to everything from day one actually prevents you from understanding how the engine works.

What is one piece of expensive software you think people rely on too much?
approved.reasoning: Focuses on the early days of his e-commerce ventures, emphasizing the 'scrappy' student-founder mindset of learning by doing.

approved.post_text:
My code broke in production while I was in the middle of a lecture.

Getting a notification that your site is down while you are sitting in a classroom is a specific kind of stress. You have to decide whether to leave the class or wait until the break to debug.

I realized that my error handling for the checkout flow was not catching edge cases when the internet connection dropped momentarily. The state management in my frontend logic was assuming the server would always respond in under a second.

It taught me that real-world users do not have the stable fiber-optic connections we enjoy during development. Reliability is often more about how you handle the failure than how well the code runs in perfect conditions.

How do you handle urgent production fixes when you are physically occupied elsewhere?
approved.reasoning: Highlights the reality of being a student-founder in Bangalore, balancing academics with live product maintenance.

approved.post_text:
I stopped trying to perfect my designs before launching them.

Early on, I spent weeks tweaking border radiuses and button shadows for STRAYED. I thought that if the site looked perfect, customers would trust the brand immediately.

Then I looked at the actual conversion data. The time I spent on visual polish made zero difference to the people who were just trying to find the size guide or the shipping policy.

Functionality and clear information always beat a pretty interface in a direct comparison. I started shipping the design updates in small batches instead of waiting for a total site overhaul.

When was the last time you prioritized form over function and regretted it?
approved.reasoning: Shares a professional growth lesson regarding UX and design vs. actual business utility.

approved.post_text:
Working on two brands at once meant I had to stop context switching.

I used to jump between Prettiva and Co and STRAYED every single hour. I felt busy, but I was not actually making any progress on either.

I switched to themed days. One brand gets my full focus on Mondays and Wednesdays, while the other gets Tuesdays and Thursdays. Fridays are for whatever is burning the hottest.

My output doubled because I stopped wasting time loading mental state every time I opened a new project directory.

How do you manage your focus when you have multiple competing priorities?

Building a brand from a dorm room is mostly about fixing broken logistics.

People see the website and the products, but they do not see the hours spent talking to courier partners about why a package is stuck at a hub. It is the most unglamorous part of running a business.

I learned more about supply chain management by troubleshooting delivery failures than I ever would have in a classroom. Every delay was a lesson in setting customer expectations.

Sometimes the technology works perfectly, but the physical world is the bottleneck. You have to build the software to account for that reality.

What is the most unexpected challenge you faced when starting your own project?
approved.reasoning: Shows the contrast between the digital world he builds and the physical logistics of his retail brands.

I spent three days hunting a bug that only appeared on mobile web.

It was one of those issues that worked perfectly on my local environment and on desktop browsers. But on mobile, the checkout button simply would not trigger.

I had to borrow phones from three different friends just to test various screen sizes and OS versions. It turned out to be a minor conflict between a script I added for animations and the mobile touch event listener.

Mobile users make up the bulk of our traffic, and yet I was doing 90 percent of my testing on a wide monitor. That was a humbling wake-up call about who my actual users were.

What is the weirdest bug you have ever encountered in your production code?
approved.reasoning: A technical anecdote that emphasizes user-centric development.

approved.post_text:
Most advice about building a brand ignores the cost of user trust.

When we started, I thought the goal was to get as many people to the site as possible. I was obsessed with traffic stats and vanity metrics.

Then I realized that one bad experience with a support email or a late update can undo months of marketing efforts. Trust is expensive to build and incredibly easy to lose.

Now I prioritize speed of response and honesty about delays over trying to grow the numbers at any cost. You only get one chance to make a first impression.

How do you measure the health of your customer relationships beyond just the sales numbers?
approved.reasoning: Focuses on the importance of reputation and customer service over 'growth hacking'.

approved.post_text:
I used to think my code had to be perfect to be successful.

I would spend hours refactoring components that no one would ever see. I wanted the file structure to be clean and the naming conventions to be textbook standard.

But the brands were growing, and I was holding them back by spending too much time on internal architecture. I had to learn to write code that was good enough to get the job done and reliable enough to not crash.

Technical debt is a real thing, but perfectionism is a business killer when you are moving fast. Sometimes, shipped and messy is better than never shipped and clean.

At what point do you decide that your code is good enough to deploy?
approved.reasoning: Addresses the common developer struggle of balancing clean code with product deadlines.

approved.post_text:
I almost quit Karate after 8 years.

I started learning Karate when I was around 10 years old.

For years, every Tuesday and Thursday, I'd show up to training. I went from a white belt, all the way to brown.

But somewhere along the way, I started losing interest.

As I got older, Karate just didn't feel as exciting anymore. I wanted to stop.

But my parents encouraged me to keep going.

And I remember thinking:

"If I stop now, what do I have to show for all these years?"

So I kept going.

For another year and a half, I pushed through. I eventually switched to a much more intensive training session once a week and started putting in more effort than I had before.

After around 10 years of training, I finally earned my Black Belt. 🥋

Looking back, getting the Black Belt wasn't the hardest part.

The hardest part was continuing when I didn't want to.

Karate taught me something I've found myself using in almost everything I do now:

Motivation gets you started. Commitment keeps you going.

Sometimes you don't need to love what you're doing every day.

You just need to keep showing up.

You don't need to know how you're going to achieve your goal. You just need to believe it's possible.

I've started to realize this more and more over the years.

Before starting my clothing brands, I knew almost nothing about running a business.

I didn't know how to find manufacturers. I didn't know how to source products. I didn't know how to build a brand.

I just had an idea and wanted to see if I could make it work.

When we started working on STRAYED, I didn't even know how I was going to build the website from scratch with the limitations we had.

So I figured it out.

With Prettiva & Co., we initially tried Amazon because it seemed like the easiest way to get started. Eventually, we realized it wasn't the right fit for what we wanted to do.

So we looked for other options.

We tried things, changed our approach, found solutions that worked for us, and kept moving.

And that's probably one of the biggest things I've learned from all of this:

You don't always need the answer before you start.

Sometimes you just need a goal big enough that you're willing to figure out the rest along the way.

There will be things you don't know.
There will be things that don't work.
There will be times when you have no idea what to do next.

But there's almost always another way forward.

It might take weeks. It might take months.

But if you keep looking, keep learning, and don't give up, you'll eventually find a way.

So dream big.

Don't limit your goals based on what you think is possible today.

Set the goal first.

Figure out the how along the way.
